Expansion note: how a diode differs from a transistor

A diode has one p–n junction and primarily controls current in one direction. A transistor uses multiple semiconductor regions or a gate-controlled channel to control a larger current; the packet previews BJTs and field-effect transistors before later lessons study them in detail.

(*) We will study operation† and models† of the two types of transistors, BJT† and FET†; focus on the MOSFET† because of its widespread use† in applications.

Expansion note: why electronics spans these application areas

Analog circuits amplify or regulate continuous signals; converters translate between analog and digital representations; digital logic combines discrete 0/1 states. Each is built from devices such as diodes and transistors, so the same semiconductor physics supports the applications pictured in the packet.

L1-5

(*) We can have many† components of circuits (ICs†). An IC could have millions† of individual devices. The devices come in various packages†.

And we see that for discrete components† too†.

Moore’s Law: number of transistors† in an IC† doubles† about every 2† years.

→ The removal of heat† imposes a limit to size of transistors.

Expansion note: what Moore’s Law describes

Moore’s Law is a historical trend in the number of transistors that could be integrated on a chip, often summarized as a doubling about every two years. It is an observation about integration density, not a physical law that guarantees smaller transistors indefinitely. Heat removal and power density are practical design limits.

L1-6

Semiconductor Physics

(*) It all starts with the atom† and its simplest model.

(*) Each shell† has a different energy† level; with those closer† to the nucleus, the lower the energy†. Each shell holds a maximum of 2n²† electrons. The outermost shell is known as the valence† shell. Electrons must receive sufficient energy to move† between energy levels†.

Expansion note: how the shell number sets its maximum electron count

The simple shell-capacity rule is 2n2, where n is the principal shell number. For the first four shells this gives 2, 8, 18 and 32 electrons. Silicon has 14 electrons, arranged 2, 8 and 4 in its occupied shells; the four outer electrons are its valence electrons.

L1-7

(*) Let’s connect this to the periodic table.

Period Number = Number of electron shells†.

Group Number = Number of valence electrons†.

Semiconductors: materials whose conductivity† can vary between conductors† and insulators†.

(*) We focus on the Group IV† elements and materials made from Groups III† & V† like GaAs†.

(*) Silicon (Si)† is our favorite semiconductor material because it is abundant† and widely available†. It has 14† electrons arranged in 3† shells in a crystal† lattice. It has 4† valence electrons — half† full.

Expansion note: interpret the group-number shortcut carefully

For the main-group columns used in this introduction, the number of valence electrons follows the group pattern: Groups 1–2 have 1–2, and Groups 13–18 have 3–8 (helium is the familiar exception). The packet’s shortcut “group number = valence electrons” refers to that main-group pattern, not every periodic-table column.

L1-8

(*) Carbon† is similar, but it takes too much energy† to free electrons† and facilitate current† flow.

(*) An Si atom looks like a central silicon atom with four valence electrons†.

So the four† empty valence-electron spots are filled by neighboring atoms† through covalent† bonds.

At 0† K, all covalent bonds are intact and electrons are not free for conduction†.

Expansion note: why carbon is not the usual semiconductor here

Carbon and silicon are both Group IV elements with four valence electrons. In diamond-like carbon, the bandgap is much larger than silicon’s, so far more energy is needed to excite electrons into mobile conduction states. Silicon’s smaller bandgap makes carrier generation practical at ordinary temperatures.

L1-9

(*) As temperature increases†, sufficient thermal energy† exists to break† some of the bonds. Freeing an electron into the conduction† band leaves behind a hole† in the atom, implying a positive† charge and attracting other electrons†.

So you have movement of both electrons† in the conduction† band and holes† in the valence† band.

(*) Creating carriers by increasing temperature is called thermal generation†. Some of the free electrons† fill holes†; this is called recombination†.

(*) In thermal equilibrium†, generation = recombination.

So if concentration is in equilibrium†, then n and p concentrations are stable.

Then for Si and T = 300† K, n_i† = n_0 = p_0† = 1.5×1010 carriers/cm³.

Noting that Si has 5×1022 atoms/cm³!

Expansion note: what a thermally generated hole represents

When a valence electron gains enough energy to enter the conduction band, it leaves an unoccupied valence-band state. That vacancy is the hole. The electron and hole are created as a pair; later recombination removes one of each.

Q. How convert bandgap energy to photon wavelength?

Expansion note: use consistent energy and temperature units

The exponent is dimensionless when Eg and kT use the same energy unit. With Eg in electron-volts, use k=8.62×10−5eV/K and absolute temperature in kelvins. The stated B units make ni a concentration per cubic centimeter.

L1-11

(*) Recall E=hcλ†.

h = 6.626×10−34 J·s; c = 2.998×108 m/s.

So hc = 1240† eV·nm.

So λnm=1240eV\,nmEgeV†.

For E_g = 1.46 eV → λ = 849† nm.

Doping: significantly changes† carrier concentrations by introducing impurity† atoms without changing the crystal properties.

n-type → Si doped with Group V†, like phosphorus†.

p-type → Si doped with Group III†, like boron†.

(*) If we make concentration of donor† atoms N_D much greater† than n_i, then n_n ≈ N_D†.

And since n_n p_n = n_i²†.

Expansion note: connect photon energy and wavelength

A photon carries energy E=hc/λ. Combining h and c with electron-volt and nanometer units gives the convenient approximation hc≈1240eV\,nm, so a 1.46 eV bandgap corresponds to λ≈1240/1.46=849nm, just beyond the visible red range.

Expansion note: why donor doping makes silicon n-type

A Group V atom has one more valence electron than silicon. It can donate that extra electron to the conduction band, making electrons the majority carriers. A Group III acceptor has one fewer valence electron and creates a hole, making holes the majority carriers.

L1-12

We can solve for

pn≈ni2nn=ni2ND=(1.5×1010cm^{-3})21017cm^{-3}=2.25×103cm^{-3}.†

Ex. n-type Si at 300 K has N_D = 1017/cm³. Find p_n.

Expansion note: use the mass-action relation for minority carriers

At equilibrium, nnpn=ni2. Since donor concentration is much larger than the intrinsic concentration, nn≈ND. Therefore pn≈ni2/ND, which evaluates to 2.25×103cm^{-3} for the values printed in these notes.

Appendix

A. Problem Types in This Notetaker and How to Solve Them

A1. Find photon wavelength from bandgap energy

Recognize it: the bandgap is given in eV and the question asks for the photon wavelength.

Method:

  1. Use E=hc/λ.
  2. With hc≈1240eV\,nm, compute λnm=1240/Eg.
  3. State the wavelength in nm and locate it relative to the visible band if asked.

Check: higher photon energy must correspond to shorter wavelength. For 1.46 eV, λ≈849 nm.

Common mistakes: mixing joules with electron-volts; using kelvins in a wavelength calculation; inverting the ratio.

Worked in these notes: L1-11.

A2. Find minority-carrier concentration in doped silicon

Recognize it: dopant concentration and intrinsic concentration are given, and the requested carrier is the minority carrier.

Method:

  1. For n-type silicon with donors, set nn≈ND when ND≫ni.
  2. Apply equilibrium mass action, nnpn=ni2.
  3. Solve pn≈ni2/ND, carrying concentration units consistently.

Check: the minority concentration should be far below the majority concentration; the product should recover ni2. For the printed example, pn=2.25×103cm^{-3}.

Common mistakes: confusing donor density with hole density, forgetting to square ni, or omitting the per-cubic-centimeter units.

Worked in these notes: L1-9 and L1-12.

A3. Classify a doped silicon sample

Recognize it: the impurity species or dopant group is specified.

Method: Group V donors (for example, phosphorus) add electrons and create n-type material; Group III acceptors (for example, boron) create holes and p-type material. Identify the majority carrier, then identify the other type as minority.

Check: donor doping must make electrons the majority; acceptor doping must make holes the majority.

Common mistakes: labeling the sample by the dopant’s charge instead of the majority carrier.

Worked in these notes: L1-11.

B. Topics Covered by the Lesson 1 Notes

B1. Electronics and electronic devices
  • Electronic applications in consumer products, vehicles and defense systems (L1-3).
  • Analog functions, data conversion and digital logic (L1-4).
  • Diodes, transistor types and integrated-circuit internals (L1-1, L1-4).
  • Integrated-circuit and discrete-device package examples (L1-5).
  • Moore’s Law and the practical thermal limit on transistor scaling (L1-5).
B2. Atoms, shells and semiconductor materials
  • Electron shells, energy levels, valence shells, orbitals and subshell capacities (L1-6).
  • Period and group patterns in the periodic table (L1-7 to L1-8).
  • Silicon’s four valence electrons and covalent bonds (L1-7 to L1-8).
  • Bandgap energy and the distinction between silicon and wide-bandgap carbon (L1-8, L1-10).
B3. Carriers, thermal generation and equilibrium
  • Conduction-band electrons and valence-band holes (L1-8 to L1-9).
  • Thermal generation and electron-hole recombination (L1-9).
  • Intrinsic carrier concentration in silicon and mass action (L1-9 to L1-10).
  • Photon energy, bandgap and wavelength (L1-10 to L1-11).
B4. Doping and carrier concentration
  • Group V donor doping and n-type silicon (L1-11).
  • Group III acceptor doping and p-type silicon (L1-11).
  • Majority/minority carrier approximations and minority-carrier concentration (L1-11 to L1-12).

C. Equations Used Throughout

C1. Shell and orbital capacity

Shell capacity: Nshell,max=2n2. An orbital holds two electrons. Subshell orbital counts: s=1, p=3, d=5, f=7; their maximum electron counts are 2, 6, 10 and 14.

C2. Intrinsic concentration and equilibrium carriers

Intrinsic concentration: ni=BT3/2e−Eg/(2kT). Thermal equilibrium mass action: nnpn=ni2. For n-type silicon with ND≫ni: nn≈ND,pn≈ni2ND.

C3. Photon energy and wavelength

E=hcλhc≈1240eV\,nmλnm≈1240EeV.
